Setup and connections

Native setup wizard, account connections, model selection, and the private app-management protocol.

About 10 min read · 8 sections

On this page
01 Connecting accounts and servers 02 Existing connections 03 Shared-gateway clients 04 Configuration and credential ownership 05 Private management transport 06 Verification 07 Verified on October 23, 2026 08 Verified on October 18, 2026

A new installation opens the setup wizard. An existing valid configuration opens the normal app and its configured connections. The wizard can also be opened from Add connection or Settings.

The wizard guides the user through choosing a provider, connecting the account or server, selecting models, and reviewing the connection. It stages changes privately until Apply connection is selected. First setup then uses the gateway's existing service and desktop-registration commands. The final screen reports those results separately and offers another setup attempt if needed. Initial desktop registration takes effect when Codex is quit and reopened once.

Connecting accounts and servers

Claude and Copilot can use the vendor CLI's existing sign-in when the user explicitly selects that option. A separate account uses its own authentication directory. New browser sign-in uses the official CLI's subscription login flow. Missing provider CLIs have links to their installation instructions.

Codex uses the gateway's separate Sign in with ChatGPT registration. It does not copy the native Codex account's authentication. An optional account email restricts the new registration to that account, and reconnecting a stored account retains its verified identity restriction. Codex authentication and catalog discovery use HTTP; they do not require a separate Codex CLI installation.

To add an account that is also used natively, add a separate Codex connection and sign in with that account's email. Each Mac gets its own gateway registration; native credentials and rotating refresh tokens are not copied between machines. The account-qualified gateway aliases remain distinct from the native models. When adding a second Codex account, preserve the previous bare-model route by explicitly designating the existing account with defaultForBareModels: true unless the operator requests a different default. Otherwise a formerly unique bare subagent model can become ambiguous. See account routing. Native picker selection is separate from each gateway connection's enabled models; see native picker selection.

Responses, Anthropic, and OpenAI-compatible servers accept a server URL and an API key. HTTP is limited to loopback. An unauthenticated local server can leave the key empty; the app stores an unused local credential to satisfy the existing gateway configuration contract. HTTPS servers require a supplied key. Servers that do not expose a model catalog support explicit model IDs.

Named API presets cover Grok/xAI, OpenCode Console, OpenCode Go and OpenRouter. They use the existing API transports and credential storage. OpenCode connections select the model's native API format. See API providers for endpoints, model selection and the distinction between API credits and Grok subscription usage.

New configurations prefer loopback port 3457 and select an available loopback port when it is already occupied. Existing configurations retain their port. Creating a connection does not restart an existing service.

Existing connections

For opt-in updates of only the families already selected, use Automatic latest models. New unrelated models stay visible but unchecked, and older chat routes remain usable after leaving the picker. See automatic latest models for the five-minute schedule, provider dates, baseline and safety rules.

The host view identifies This Mac and its computer name. Its connections and model selections belong to that Mac. A Codex SSH chat uses the gateway on the remote execution host, not the gateway on the Mac displaying the chat.

Connections shows each provider's label, configured model count, and available authentication evidence. Saved credentials are distinguished from a successful model-catalog check. Catalog checks do not send inference prompts.

Users can check a connection, refresh its catalog, choose enabled models, rename it, reconnect an account, or replace an app-managed API key. Externally managed credentials remain outside these editing controls. Removing a connection keeps its credentials and requires confirmation; the last provider cannot be removed.

Use Move up and Move down on a connection to save a custom order, or choose Move to top from its menu. The first connection appears first in the app and among gateway provider groups in the model catalog. Native model rows retain their separate position. Ordering does not change the selected model, account routing, or the designated account for bare subagent model names. It applies on that gateway host, so reorder each host separately when using several Macs. Shared clients display their host's order without local editing controls.

Native GPT fallback models separately controls the local adapter's native fallback rows: First, Last, or Hidden. Last keeps them visible below the gateway groups. Hidden removes them only from the normal picker; it does not disable native chats, explicit model requests, or account authentication. The existing native model selection stays unchanged. Current registered adapters apply a saved change on the next picker refresh; older adapters first need normal reconnection to load this behavior. The app never restarts active chats to apply a preference.

Shared clients may edit this local native picker preference even though their remote provider catalog is read-only. It belongs to the execution host's own configuration, not to the shared inference host. SSH chats use the remote Mac's preference. See native picker placement.

Refreshing a catalog does not change enabled routes. Applying a selection keeps every existing alias and its metadata for retained upstream models. A private alias ledger reserves retired route identities, so another model or account cannot silently take an alias referenced by saved chats.

Existing Grok subscription connections keep the sign-in state of the gateway's private Grok home: the connection reports whether auth.json exists and whether the grok CLI is installed. Reconnect runs that CLI's device-code login against the same home, and the app treats a clean exit as success only once the credential file exists. Their configured models can be disabled and re-enabled without losing their aliases or metadata. Grok has no catalog discovery, so Refresh stays unavailable.

Shared-gateway clients

A configuration with clientOnly: true shows a read-only shared catalog instead of local connection editors. The source name comes from the serving gateway, not the client's computer name or a cached catalog. Provider credentials and model-selection changes remain on that host.

Inspection uses the existing private stateDirectory/client-token to request GET /v1/gateway-info through the configured loopback port or SSH forward. This authenticated endpoint returns only protocol version, serving hostname, provider IDs/labels/types, and selected model IDs/labels. It exposes no credentials, configuration paths, or authentication evidence and sends no inference request. An unavailable, incompatible, or invalid response clears the shared catalog and offers a retry; it never displays a previous host's catalog as current. The read has a three-second network deadline and a 1 MiB body limit, with at most 32 providers and 256 models per provider. A catalog exceeding those protocol bounds is refused whole, not silently truncated.

Configuration and credential ownership

The app reads the configuration used by the managed service or the explicit file selected in Advanced settings. Each edit carries the revision that was reviewed. A changed revision is refused under the configuration lock and must be refreshed. Unknown configuration fields and unrelated providers are preserved. A private backup is saved before a changed existing configuration is atomically replaced. An unchanged selection leaves the original file untouched.

New connections own private credential and authentication directories under the gateway state directory. Configuration, draft, backup, and credential files use owner-only permissions. Directory ancestry and ownership are checked before writes, and symlink escapes are refused. No configuration edit writes native Codex authentication, model choices, agent instructions, roles, or permissions.

Cancellation stops the app-owned management process and its attached helpers. The wizard does not reuse an earlier failed or cancelled draft. Uncommitted private state may remain on disk; cancelling does not delete existing credentials or publish its staged routes.

Private management transport

The app launches its bundled Node runtime with Contents/Resources/management/dist/app-management.js. One bounded JSON request travels over standard input and one typed JSON response returns on standard output. API keys are never command arguments or environment values. Child output and raw exceptions are not displayed or logged.

The operations are inspect, prepare, authenticate, discover, commit, models, rename, reorder, native-picker, auto-latest, auto-latest-check, remove, discard, and the read-only activity operation. Activity reports existing local executors and saved outcomes without starting or resuming a chat; see execution activity. auto-latest saves a boolean enabled with the reviewed revision, capturing today's selected families without changing model selection. auto-latest-check uses the reviewed revision to run one metadata-only check. Both report the effective policy and bounded check/scheduling status. Automatic checks run inside the existing signed app-owned service. A toggle never adds a LaunchAgent; the live heartbeat reports when that service has adopted maintenance. Legacy 0.8.7 metadata jobs are retired without editing the parent app's registration or interrupting chats. Reordering sends providerIds, an exact permutation of all local connection IDs, together with the reviewed configuration revision. Duplicate, missing, or unknown IDs and outdated revisions are refused. An unchanged order does not rewrite the file. native-picker saves nativeModelPickerPlacement with the reviewed revision, using the same private backup and atomic save. It preserves all other fields and providers. Saving the effective default first to an unchanged implicit default does not rewrite the configuration. The TypeScript types in src/app-management/types.ts and Swift types in GatewayManagementTypes.swift define the protocol. Requests are limited to 128 KiB and responses to 2 MiB. Ordinary operations have a thirty-second deadline; interactive authentication has fifteen minutes. Input, output, cancellation, and timeout cleanup are bounded.

The management module set is packaged with the app independently of the existing inference release. Updating the control panel preserves the installed gateway command, running daemon, native components, and their release ownership. Validation and discovery use the verified engine libraries bundled with the app. This preserves registered transport options such as Tailnet routes, while new wizard inputs retain the stricter HTTPS-or-loopback URL checks. A packaged app with missing or invalid engine libraries fails closed. Source-only tests use the repository's local libraries.

Verification

Run the normal gateway gate and the native checks:

npm run build
npm run check
npm test
npm run app:test
npm run app:e2e -- --output /tmp/harness-wizard-verification
npm run app:e2e:connections -- --output /tmp/harness-connections-verification

The end-to-end runner uses a real isolated gateway and a loopback model server. It checks creation, discovery, selected-model persistence, actual Responses translation, API-key replacement, concurrent-edit refusal, and unchanged native account sentinels. No paid provider inference is used.

The connections runner checks all four subscription/API provider fixtures, Grok model-selection roundtrips, an authenticated shared catalog, read-only client behavior, and clearing the catalog when its gateway becomes unavailable. It also supports --serve-fixture for host/client GUI verification.

For rendered first-run verification, start the same fixture with --serve-fixture. Its JSON metadata identifies the new private home, target configuration, and local server. Launch the built app with:

open -n "/absolute/path/GateFox.app" --args \
  --config /absolute/fixture/home/settings/gateway.json \
  --data-home /absolute/fixture/home

Use the actual configPath and home printed by the fixture. Explicit launches have separate gateway-selection preferences. The data home must be a private directory owned by the current user, and the configuration must be inside it. Invalid, duplicate, or malformed options fail before the app loads normal user state.

The GUI fixture substitutes only the macOS service-registration boundary. Its service command starts the real gateway against the configuration saved by the wizard. It does not register a LaunchAgent or change the live desktop adapter. After testing, quit the fixture app and stop the fixture coordinator, then reopen the normal installed app.

Verified on October 23, 2026

The real native Connections screen displayed the four-provider host fixture, including Grok, and identified the local Mac and SSH execution scope. The Grok model sheet offered configured checkboxes without discovery or manual model inputs. Disabling, applying, reopening, and re-enabling a model restored the configuration's exact original SHA-256 digest.

The client-only fixture displayed the actual serving hostname and all four providers without credential controls. Stopping only the fixture gateway and refreshing removed the old provider rows and displayed the unavailable/retry state. These checks used local mocks, not paid inference or live service changes. Automated coverage also checks duplicate Grok aliases with distinct metadata, private-home isolation, bounded hostile shared responses, and obsolete refreshes after same-path cancellation or an A-to-B-to-A configuration switch.

Verified on October 18, 2026

The MacBook GUI completed a fresh local-server setup, discovered two models, saved one selected model, and reached the ready screen. The configuration did not exist before Apply. A real Responses request through that saved gateway returned the local test model's response.

The same GUI test changed the configured selection to two models, replaced its private API key, renamed the connection, added and removed a second connection, and reopened the saved configuration without repeating first-run setup. The last-provider removal guard was checked.

The corrected app was installed on Studio and MacBook. Their installed native management bridge loaded the real configurations: two providers and twenty models on Studio, three providers and twenty-one models on MacBook. Discovery through the MacBook's registered Tailnet Qwen connection succeeded. Configuration digests and running gateway PIDs remained unchanged across the app updates.

Browser and device-code login wrappers, cancellation, private authentication homes, and identity restrictions have isolated automated coverage. The live account checks reused the existing registrations and did not perform fresh browser consent or paid provider inference. The MacBook screen locked after the GUI walkthrough; the final transport compatibility correction was checked through the installed native bridge and management backend.
